tier_reason: The README table (v1.0.0) times Notorious-FFT against minfft in the same binary built from the public benchmarks/bench.c (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, warm-up, 100-100000 reps); it names the compiler (GCC 11.4.0), flags (-O3 -march=armv8.2-a+fp16) and CPU (Cortex-A78AE, Jetson Orin), so it meets A. Every number in claimed_speedup appears in the table.

corrections.caveats: Baseline minfft is a small niche library (53 stars), not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT; margins are 8-13% on complex DFT and 1-7% on real DFT, with losses at N=16-64 for real DFT and DCT-2. Only an ARM machine is measured; the AVX2/AVX-512 paths have no published numbers. The README names a comprehensive benchmark against FFTW3, KissFFT, PocketFFT and muFFT but publishes no results. The core is minfft-compatible (header comments: same split-radix 2/4 structure and twiddle layout as minfft's rs_dft_1d); the README does not credit minfft. The same author's FastAndFourier benchmarks/README.md gives two KissFFT comparisons: on an x86_64 AVX2 Mac (2026-02-22, older build) Notorious-FFT was slower than KissFFT at every size (0.57-0.76x relative throughput) and 10-17x behind FFTW_MEASURE; on Linux aarch64 (2026-09-03, v1.0.1) it beat KissFFT at every size (e.g. N=1024 13.8 vs 21.7 us, N=65536 1620 vs 2735 us). A Bluestein AVX inverse-twiddle double-conjugation bug was fixed on 2026-08-22, after the v1.0.0 release.

notes: Numbers and metadata check out (MIT, 0 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-22). Tier A rests on a weak baseline (minfft); the FastAndFourier README shows it losing to KissFFT on x86 and beating it on aarch64, worth recording as a shortcoming.

tier_reason: docs/related.rst compares FINUFFT against NFFT3, CMCL and MIRT and points to the peer-reviewed SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 41(5) C479-C504 (2019) paper, whose abstract (seen via a search result; arXiv itself is blocked here) reports favorable speed and memory against several popular CPU NUFFT libraries, especially in 3-D. The nufft-bench harness is public, but FINUFFT flags and CPU are not stated there, so B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/related.rst: NFFT 'significantly slower and/or more memory-intensive than FINUFFT'; CMCL NUFFT 'much (up to 50x even for one thread) slower'; MIRT 'slower than FINUFFT for all tolerances smaller than 10^-1'; DUCC 'in some regimes is faster than ours'; NonuniformFFTs.jl 'close to our CPU performance, and can beat it in the case of real data'. Paper abstract (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2019): favorable speed and memory footprint against several popular CPU libraries, especially in three dimensions. Legacy cuFINUFFT README (flatironinstitute/cufinufft): acceleration over FINUFFT of up to 10x and up to 100x faster than other established GPU NUFFT codes.
corrections.caveats: The tier B rests on the peer-reviewed 2019 paper; its full text could not be opened here (arXiv and Semantic Scholar blocked), only its abstract via a search result. ahbarnett/nufft-bench says MIRT's apply step beats all others in 1-D and 2-D, while MIRT precomputation is very expensive. DUCC is faster in some regimes, and NonuniformFFTs.jl is close on CPU, beats it on real data and claims its GPU type 1 beats cuFINUFFT v2.4.1. Library comparisons date from 2018-2019; docs/performance.rst only tracks FINUFFT against its own releases. Baselines are other NUFFT codes, not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT, and the fit with the FFT category is loose.

notes: Quotes on related.rst, the nufft-bench compiler notes and the cuFINUFFT 10x/100x line all verified; Apache-2.0, 445 stars, last commit 2026-09-30 confirmed. Mixed picture against DUCC (already filed in wave 8) and NonuniformFFTs.jl is worth recording.

tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark harness (benchmarks/) with tables in the README and benchmarks/README.md against KissFFT and FFTW3. Flags are given, but no compiler name and no CPU model on either machine (only '16 x 2300 MHz x86_64 AVX2' and 'aarch64 6 x 1728 MHz'), so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: x86 run: Release build -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, FP64 for all libraries (README and benchmarks/README.md; the README says Release builds also add -funroll-loops). aarch64 run: Release -O3 -march=native. Compiler name and version not stated.
corrections.hardware: x86_64 macOS Ventura (Darwin 22.6.0), 16 x 2300 MHz, AVX2, no AVX-512, L3 16 MiB; Linux aarch64 6 x 1728 MHz, L1 64 KiB, L2 256 KiB x 6, L3 2 MiB, CPU frequency scaling on. CPU models not named.
corrections.caveats: The README says FFTW3 FFTW_MEASURE wins at nearly every size and that small N was not its race on x86. On x86 the win over KissFFT appears only at N=65536 (907 vs 3253 us); FAF is 2.5-4x slower than KissFFT from N=64 to 16384 (derived from page data). On aarch64 it beats KissFFT at N=8 and from N=32 upward but loses at N=16. The benchmarks README is inconsistent: its two x86 small-N tables disagree (N=16 FAF 1.72 us vs 1330 ns, KissFFT 0.210 us vs 72.6 ns); the 2026-02-22 run claims NotoriousFFT pinned to v1.0.1, a release made in August 2026; and the 'FAF vs FFTW3 3.01x' cell at N=65536 is FAF being 3x slower. The x86 run used -ffast-math. The aarch64 run had frequency scaling on. NotoriousFFT, by the same author, is 1.2-2.15x faster than FAF on aarch64. It is a separate JIT/VM codebase, not a duplicate of Notorious-FFT.

notes: All claimed numbers are on the README and benchmarks/README.md; MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-25 confirmed. Not a duplicate of Notorious-FFT (different engine, same author), but a weak entry: a win only at 65536 on x86 and modest wins on aarch64, with internal table inconsistencies.
